Dear Acting Administrator Wheeler, 

On behalf of the Business for Innovative Climate and Energy 

Policy Network (BICEP), I hereby submit comments on the 

Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) Notice of Proposed 

Rule for the Protection of Stratospheric Ozone: Revisions to the 

Refrigerant Management Program’s Extension to Substitutes. 

The proposal rolls back a 2016 extension of the appliance 

maintenance and leak repair provisions at 40 CFR 82.157 to 

appliances using only non-exempt substitute refrigerants, and 

seeks comment on whether to withdraw the extension of the full 

set of subpart F provisions to non-exempt substitute 

refrigerants.

BICEP is a coalition of 52 businesses from a broad range of 

industry sectors, united in advocating for stronger climate and 

clean energy policies at the state and federal level. On behalf of 

BICEP, I strongly encourage the EPA to maintain the extension 

of the maintenance and leak repair provisions, as well as the 

broader extension throughout subpart F of 40 CFR 82. The 

proposed rule changes offer little economic benefit, create a 

discontinuity between state and federal policy, and work against 

the business community’s climate goals. In addition, I argue that 

EPA did not exceed its statutory authority in extending the rules 

to non-exempt substitutes. 

Minimal Economic Benefit

The economic arguments in favor of the proposed rule are 

unrealistic and in any case fail to offer substantial benefit. 

According to the EPA’s cost analysis, the proposal generates all 

of its savings from reducing the compliance burden of impacted 

companies. These savings are lessened somewhat by the fact 

that under the proposal more equipment will leak refrigerant 

more often. The EPA estimates this additional cost at nearly $15 

million per year, for an effective savings of just over $24 million.

Regarding: Comments on proposed revisions to regulations that implement the Federal Seed Act (FSA) 

The American Seed Trade Association (ASTA) is submitting these comments on the currently pending 

amendments to the regulations that implement the Federal Seed Act on behalf of our membership. The 

association has held multiple meetings among a broad representation of our membership to ensure their 

input and consensus to this comment letter. We also appreciate the agency’s willingness to coordinate 

communication between all facets of the seed industry to ensure awareness and interaction. It is our 

opinion that all facets of the seed industry are aware of these suggested changes and have had the 

opportunity to comment. 

Founded in 1883, ASTA is one of the oldest trade organizations in the United States. Its membership 

consists of over 700 companies involved in seed production and distribution, plant breeding, and related 

industries. ASTA is a diverse organization – it represents all types of seed companies and technologies – 

seed from alfalfa to zucchini, technologies from organic to biotechnology, and companies from “mom and 

pop” to multinationals. It works on behalf of all of its members at the state, national, and international 

levels. In other words, ASTA represents every seed company that would be affected by the proposed 

amendments, in addition to the rest of agribusiness and consumers, whom the proposed amendments 

would ultimately benefit. 

Our comments and suggestions are below. Thank you for your consideration. 

General Comment 

ASTA COMMENT: Our comments are based on the unique characteristics of the subsets of the industry 

including the vegetable and conservation seed sectors. It is apparent that these proposed changes 

attempt to integrate vegetable seeds toward similar regulations as crop seeds. An example of one 

significant issue is that vegetable seed is generally sold by count, not weight. That issue complicates and 

conflicts with the general concept of these changes, and are noted throughout our comments. Before the 

integration of any rules affecting vegetable seeds, the regulations should consider correcting and 

clarifying the count vs. weight issues that have arisen in several parts of the rules as a result of these 

proposed changes, in addition to further consideration of other aspects of the segments that are affected.

Thanks for the opportunity to comment on the proposed regulations. I ask that you extend the comment period until March 1 of 2022 and postpone action of any of these proposals until the fishers of the Northeast area have had time to thoroughly peruse these proposals and then comment. Asking for comment during the height of the summer fishing season is a disservice to the fishers that you serve. We serious watermen and women are on the water daily from June through October and the comment process is a cumbersome process for a layperson to sort through the documents at that time of year. NOAA/NMFS via HMS does not have their finger on the pulse of this fishery, as evidence by the herky jerky management of the last several years ! 
Opening the general category season this year at 3 per day was a mistake ! Then adding closed fishing days in the middle of the fishing season further indicates the regulators ARE OUT OF TOUCH with the changes this fishery has evolved into. Quota distribution has been seemingly favoring the early subquotas to the detriment of the fall participants over the last several years. It is not too late to remedy this disproportionate allocation and distribution process. Extend the comment period. Delay action of quota distribution proposals until you have seriously considered the "Wicked Tuna effect". The Charter Headboat category must have proven they do charters to qualify. General Category boats need to comply with safety regulations or show a schedule C to be "commercial". This fishery has evolved into a part time free for all with tourists and weekend warriors on vacation, filling the summer quotas with poorly cared for, low quality fish. 
It is time for NOAA/NMFS to step up and be proactive and not reactive in mamaging this fishery.

On behalf of America’s Health Insurance Plans (AHIP), we appreciate the opportunity to 

respond to the Food and Drug Administration’s (FDA) notice on research entitled, “Disclosures 

of Descriptive Presentations in Professional Oncology Prescription Drug Promotion.” 

AHIP is the national trade association representing the health insurance community. AHIP’s 

members provide health and supplemental benefits through employer-sponsored coverage, the 

individual insurance market, and public programs such as Medicare and Medicaid. AHIP’s 

members have broad experience working with hospitals, physicians, patients, employers, state 

governments, the federal government, pharmaceutical and device companies, and other 

healthcare stakeholders to ensure patients have access to needed treatments and medical services 

at an affordable price. 

The FDA is proposing to study the impact of disclosures in promotional labeling and advertising 

to health care professionals for oncology products. Specifically, the FDA is seeking to examine 

the utility of disclosures in communicating information on scientific and clinical data, (including 

data limitations) and the practical utility of the information for use in treatment. The proposed 

study seeks to address a range of questions, including whether disclosures mitigate potentially 

misleading presentations and whether technical or nontechnical disclosures are more effective 

for different types of health care professionals. 

We strongly support the FDA’s proposed study, as well as the agency’s overall research efforts 

to better understand the impact of prescription drug promotion and physician detailing and 

direct-to-consumer advertising (DTC). We agree with the FDA’s assessment that dedicated 

research is necessary regarding oncology drug promotion, particularly given that a significant 

proportion of the drug development pipeline is comprised of oncology products and that an 

increasing number of oncology drugs are approved under expedited pathways with surrogate 

endpoints.

Ohioans have gone three-and-a-half years without a provision the EPA now acknowledges is an important tool for achieving, maintaining, and enforcing air quality standards. EPA did not adequately consider public comments before it previously acted to remove it from Ohio's SIP.

Ohio has and had numerous counties with excessive levels of ambient pollution. EPA acted unlawfully when it removed the Air Nuisance Rule from Ohio's SIP without considering the effect of that removal on air quality in each of these counties. EPA is now correct in using 110(k)(6) (EPA's error correction rule) to reinstate the Air Nuisance Rule as the fastest, most direct means of restoring this critical provision to Ohio's state implementation plan.

Dear Administrator Cliff, 

On June 22, 2022, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) published in the 

Federal Register a Proposed Rule on Event Data Recorders (the “Proposed Rule’). The National 

Association of Mutual Insurance Companies (NAMIC) welcomes the opportunity to respond to this 

request for comments. 

NAMIC is the largest property/casualty insurance trade group with a diverse membership of more 

than 1,500 local, regional, and national member companies, including seven of the top 10 

property/casualty insurers in the United States. NAMIC members lead the personal lines sector 

representing 55 percent of the auto market. Through our advocacy programs we promote public 

policy solutions that benefit NAMIC member companies and the policyholders they serve and foster 

greater understanding and recognition of the unique alignment of interests between management and 

policyholders of mutual companies. 

The Proposed Rule would amend NHTSA regulations regarding Event Data Recorders (EDRs) to 

extend the EDR recording period for timed data metrics from 5 seconds of pre-crash data at a 

frequency of 2 Hz to 20 seconds of pre-crash data at a frequency of 10 Hz (i.e., increase from 2 

samples per second to 10 samples per second). The Proposed Rule begins the process of fulfilling 

the mandate of the Fixing America's Surface Transportation Act (FAST Act), Public Law 119-14 

(Dec. 4, 2015), to establish the appropriate recording period in NHTSA's EDR regulation. 

As detailed in the Proposed Rule, Section 24303 of the FAST Act requires NHTSA to conduct a 

study “to determine the amount of time event data recorders installed in passenger motor vehicles 

should capture and record for retrieval [of] vehicle-related data in conjunction with an event in order

 
to provide sufficient information to investigate the cause of motor vehicle crashes,” and to submit a 

report containing the findings of this study to Congress. Further, within two years of submitting this 

report to Congress, NHTSA “shall promulgate regulations to establish the appropriate period during 

which event data recorders installed in passenger motor vehicles may capture and record for retrieval 

vehicle-related data to the time necessary to provide accident investigators with vehicle-related 

information pertinent to crashes involving such motor vehicles.” 

Based upon a study to determine the frequency with which EDRs with a 5-second recording duration 

fail to record a sufficient duration of pre-crash data to determine crash causation for rear-end, 

intersection, and roadway departure crashes, NHTSA concluded that in many cases, the 5-second 

recording duration may not be sufficient to determine the factors that led to the crash or the pre-crash 

actions taken by the driver to avoid the collision, meaning that EDRs currently would not always 

provide investigators crash-related information that could assist in the determination of crash 

causation. 

Based upon a further study to determine an appropriate EDR recording duration to provide crash 

investigators with sufficient data to determine crash causation, the results of this analysis supported 

that a recording time of 15 seconds would capture approximately 50 percent of the total intersection 

event time, and 18.6 seconds would capture 90 percent. The study concluded that a recording time of 

20 seconds would capture approximately 99 percent of the total intersection event time. Based on the 

studies, NHTSA believes it is reasonable to propose requiring a minimum of 20 seconds of pre-crash 

data.

The Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) welcomes the opportunity to comment on Model
Minimum Uniform Crash Criteria (MMUCC) 5th Edition Second Online Forum. This comment specifically
regards the update of the proposed new data element on vehicle automation, as outlined in the online
document published September 16, 2016 and in the Federal Register notice on October 7, 2016.
It is unreasonable to expect police officers to accurately code a vehicle’s level of automation at crash
scenes. For example, the optional “Autopilot” feature on the Tesla Model S is implemented strictly as a
software update. So there is no way to tell if a vehicle has the option simply by visual inspection. Even
for vehicles with standard automation systems, it is not clear that officers can reliably identify the level.
Simply asking drivers also is not a reliable source because they may be driving a borrowed vehicle,
unfamiliar with optional equipment, or unresponsive due to the crash. As the complexity of such systems
grows, even knowledgeable drivers may be unable to accurately gauge the level of their vehicles’
systems. Moreover, there is no information available to link to the crash file because such optional
features are not coded in vehicle identification numbers, currently there is no requirement to code their
use in event data recorders, and owner’s manuals often include information on all available options rather
than just fitted options.
The danger of collecting inaccurate information is that some researchers will analyze it without careful
regard to or knowledge of its inaccuracy, and thus draw faulty conclusions about the state of automated
vehicles.
For these reasons, we recommend that MMUCC omit the vehicle automation data element entirely.
Sincerely,

I agree with NOAA's proposed changes to the duration of certain permits and letters of confirmation under the MMPA. I have been significantly involved in marine mammal research permits as a CI for more than 30 years and a permit holder for more than 20 years. I have worked closely with the NMFS Office of Protected Resoures on many permit related issues, and have spent a great deal of time over the years on applications, modifications, reports, and other communications with the OPR Office. I strongly believe that NOAA should be able to consider various factors when determining the appropriate duration of a given permit permit. These include the experience and track record of the applicant, the type of research to be conducted, the self-evaluation conducted during annual reports, the support of an institutional animal welfare or research committee to oversee the activity, and more. In particular, the current 5 year permit review cycle does not make sense for marine mammals that participate in long-term research programs that extend beyond the duration of the permit, or research programs that primarily conduct low-impact, behavioral studies. I have found the personnel at the Office of Protected Resources to have considerable and valuable expertise in marine mammal science and welfare. The OPR program is capable of using that expertise to make reasonable decisions about the appropriate duration of various permits. Anyone who has received a marine mammal research permit will acknowledge that it is an aurdous process with many checks and balances. Once issued, permits are updated continuously with annual reports and detailed modifications that account for any needed changes to the original permit. There is an extremely rigorous system for confirming the qualifications and experience of all personnel involved, and personnel changes are kept updated through regular modification requests. To receive a permit, input is provided from a variety of internal references and external groups including the Marine Mammal Commission, participating native co-management organizations, attending veterinarians, government partners, and other stakeholders. For many purposes including long-term research programs, it simply does not make sense to restart this process from scratch every 3-5 years. Increasing flexibility in permit durations would lower the administrative burden on scientists and increase resources available for research and education. In a research program like mine, this could amount to saving many weeks and months of time over the duration of the activity. NOAA's OPR Office has an organized and effective process for evaluating marine mammal research permit applications. This process already ensures meaningful outcomes for animal welfare under the MMPA. Increasing flexibility in the maximum duration of marine mammal research permits given by NMFS makes complete sense and I support this proposed change. Time currently spent in taxing administrative cycles with a small number of scientists can be better spent protecting marine mammals from harm at larger scales.

Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) Interpretive Statement addressing whether the Clean 
Water Act’s (“CWA” or “Act”) National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (“NPDES”) 
permit program applies to releases of pollutants from point sources to groundwater. See 84 Fed. 
Reg. 16810 (Apr. 23, 2019). We strongly support EPA’s conclusion that “the Act is best read as

coverage and liability under Section 301 of the CWA, regardless of a hydrologic connection

The undersigned organizations and our members are deeply interested in the scope and 
administration of the CWA. We represent, own, and operate facilities that are water-dependent 
enterprises. Farmers, ranchers, and foresters need to know whether their day-to-day activities are

have long had to defend against citizen suit litigation seeking to expand the scope of the NPDES

definition of point source and from there being carried to surface waters.

of the undersigned organizations are at increased risk of citizen suit enforcement. Millions of 
agricultural enterprises could be newly subject to the CWA’s permitting requirements. Equally

However, the habitats animals rely on continue to be fragmented by housing, roads, fences, energy facilities, and other man-made barriers. As a result, animals are struggling more and more to reach food, water, shelter, and breeding sites. One million animals are killed each day on American roads, and the car insurance cost to Americans is in the billions. Habitat connectivity is defined as the degree to which the landscape facilitates or impedes animal movement and other ecological processes, such as seed dispersal. And climate change is fundamentally altering landscapes, forcing many animals to relocate. As habitat continues to be fragmented, degraded, and lost to development, the need for a coordinated connectivity network is growing. Better habitat connectivity will allow wildlife to migrate and disperse throughout the country with the changing seasons, boost biodiversity and resilience in degraded ecosystems, safeguard genetic flow between populations, and ensure species are better able to adapt to our changing climate. This work is an important and long overdue investment in the long-term health of wildlife populations and ecological processes.The following are examples of current and proposed wildlife corridors:

Elk and bighorn sheep: In the Upper Rio Grande Valley, the National Wildlife Federation is working with the New Mexico Wildlife Federation, Colorado Wildlife Federation, and other partners to establish federal protections for wildlife habitat connectivity across three national forests (the Carson and Santa Fe in New Mexico, and Rio Grande in Colorado) and the Rio Grande del Norte National Monument. This corridor would help species like elk, bighorn sheep, mule deer, pronghorn, lynx, black bear, mountain lions, and the rare Rio Grande cutthroat trout.
Migrating birds and monarch butterflies: The Burnham Wildlife Corridor is a 100-acre landscape within Chicago’s Lakeshore Park featuring the prairie and woodland ecosystems that are native to this part of the Central U.S. The corridor runs right through the heart of the city. It is mainly used as a refuge for the three million migratory birds that pass through the Windy City each year, but also creates valuable butterfly habitat.
Mule deer: In Wyoming, the Red Desert to Hoback mule deer corridor supports the longest mule deer migration in the U.S.
Pronghorn and greater sage-grouse: The Northern Great Plains, which extend from Montana into Canada, support the longest pronghorn and greater sage-grouse migrations for both species. Dear Interior Secretary David Bernhart and BLM Director William Pendley:

I am writing regarding the Proposed Rule for Forest Management Decision Protest Process; 85 Fed. Reg. 34,689, June 8, 2020; RIN 1004-AE61. 

I urge you to NOT APPROVE the new rules eliminating protests for timber sales in Oregon.

It is critical that the BLM protect citizens rights to participate in decisions affecting our public lands, including timber sale protests. 

BLM lands in Oregon serve a wide variety of important public purposes that would be adversely affected by this proposed rule:
BLM forest lands in western Oregon are often intermixed with private land where people live. Logging threatens our backyard forests and the quality of life throughout western Oregon.
BLM forest lands protect watersheds. Logging threatens supplies of clean water and stable water flows.
BLM forest lands are highly productive and offer world-class capacity for carbon storage. Logging causes significant carbon emissions, and prevents forests from reaching their biological potential for climate mitigation; 
Mature forests on BLM lands are resilient to disturbance and help protect communities from fire and climate change. Logging and replanting will create dense young stands of trees that significantly increase fire hazard and are less resilient to climate change.
BLM lands provide habitat for endangered fish & wildlife and for a variety of game species. Logging impedes recovery of endangered species and reduces hunting and fish opportunities.
BLM lands offer diverse year round recreation opportunities. Logging spoils scenic views and degrades recreation experiences.
For each issue described above, the timber sale protest process helps BLM make better decisions by bringing legal and scientific missteps to the attention of the agency. The protest process also gives BLM an off-ramp from the timber sale process, so they can avoid unnecessary conflict and legal errors that lead to expensive and time-consuming litigation.

Conservation groups who commonly file timber sale protests represent tens of thousands of concerned citizens, like me, who want to see our public forests managed for clean water, ecological restoration, carbon storage, climate stability, endangered species recovery, fire resilience, recreation, and quality of life. Timber sale protests are a tool used by the public to hold public official accountable to the values we hold dear, and to environmental laws that protect them. Replacing existing protest rules with an unaccountable and very limited pre-decisional comment period will likely result in increased litigation and controversy.

Please reject this proposed rule and consider improving the existing rules so that public concerns are meaningfully addressed earlier in the process, and protests are resolved before decisions are finalized and before timber sales are auctioned. 

 
Thank you!

gender, sexual orientation, race, ethnicity, country of origin, and language interact with work 

design, management practices, and physical and psychosocial work environments in ways that 

may adversely and disproportionately affect worker safety, health, and well-being. Although the
